drills.q: Compute the parameter count of a 3x3 convolution with 128 input channels and 128 output channels, and compare it to what a fully-connected layer would cost mapping a 56x56x128 feature map to another of the same shape.
drills.a: Conv: 3*3*128*128 = 147,456 params, independent of spatial size. FC equivalent: (56*56*128)^2 ~= (401,408)^2 ~= 1.6e11 params -- roughly 6 orders of magnitude more, illustrating why weight sharing makes CNNs tractable on images.

drills.q: Compute the output size of a convolution with input 112, kernel 3, stride 1, padding 1.
drills.a: out = floor((112 + 2*1 - 3)/1) + 1 = floor(111/1) + 1 = 111 + 1 = 112. Same-padding with a 3x3 kernel and stride 1 preserves spatial size exactly, which is why it's the default choice inside residual blocks.

drills.q: Explain the degradation problem in your own words and state why it is NOT the same phenomenon as vanishing gradients in a sigmoid network.
drills.a: Adding depth to a plain (non-residual) CNN made TRAINING error worse, not just validation error, indicating an optimization failure rather than overfitting. It's not vanishing gradients in the classic sense because these networks used ReLU, which doesn't saturate on the positive side -- the actual issue was that stacked nonlinear layers struggled to learn even an identity mapping, which residual connections solve directly by providing that identity path as a default.

drills.q: You're given 50,000 labeled images for a new visual classification task and told to pick a training strategy. Would you train a ViT from scratch? Justify with the ViT paper's own findings.
drills.a: No. The ViT paper shows it underperforms comparable ResNets when trained from scratch on ImageNet-1k (~1.3M images) -- 50K images is far below even that threshold. Use a CNN (ResNet/ConvNeXt) trained from scratch or fine-tuned from ImageNet pretraining, or fine-tune (not train from scratch) a ViT that was already pretrained on a much larger corpus.

drills.q: Walk through why Faster R-CNN is faster than R-CNN, and why YOLO is faster still, in terms of what each architecture changed structurally.
drills.a: R-CNN runs each of ~2000 region proposals through a full CNN forward pass separately. Faster R-CNN shares one backbone feature extraction across the whole image and learns proposals via a Region Proposal Network on top of those shared features, eliminating the redundant per-region forward passes. YOLO removes the two-stage propose-then-classify structure entirely, directly regressing boxes and classes from a single forward pass over a grid -- no separate proposal stage at all.

drills.q: Your detector achieves strong overall mAP but performs poorly on small objects specifically. List two architectural causes and their fixes.
drills.a: Cause 1: repeated downsampling (pooling/strided convs) dilutes fine spatial detail by the time features reach the detection head -- fix with a feature pyramid network for multi-scale detection or higher input resolution. Cause 2 (if using a transformer detector like DETR): global attention dilutes local detail -- fix with a deformable/sparse-attention variant that samples locally instead of attending globally.

drills.q: Explain SAM's two-stage inference design (image encoder vs prompt encoder/mask decoder) and why it's structured that way.
drills.a: The ViT-based image encoder is the expensive part and runs exactly once per image, computing embeddings. The lightweight prompt encoder and mask decoder run per-prompt in milliseconds. This split means a user can click multiple points/boxes on the same image and get near-instant mask updates without re-running the expensive encoder each time -- the design is optimized for interactive use.

drills.q: A fine-tuned model's validation accuracy drops sharply right after you unfreeze all backbone layers and continue training at the same learning rate you used for the head. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Catastrophic forgetting: the learning rate that was appropriate for training just the new head is too high for the pretrained backbone layers, causing large updates that wipe out useful pretrained features within a few steps. Fix: use a much lower LR for fine-tuning the backbone (often 10-100x lower than head-only training), ideally with discriminative per-layer LRs and a warmup period.

drills.q: Design a segmentation strategy for a production pipeline processing 5 million images per day into a fixed set of 12 product categories. Would you use SAM directly? Justify.
drills.a: No, not as the primary model. SAM's value is zero-shot generality and interactive prompting, which isn't needed for a fixed, narrow, high-volume category set. A task-specific fine-tuned model (U-Net or Mask R-CNN trained on the 12 categories) will typically be faster and more accurate at that scale and specificity. SAM (or a SAM-distilled lightweight variant) is better suited to annotation tooling or genuinely open-vocabulary segmentation needs.

drills.q: Explain why batch norm's train-time and eval-time behavior differ, and derive the failure mode that appears when fine-tuning with a batch size of 2 on a memory-constrained GPU.
drills.a: At train time, batch norm computes mean/variance from the current mini-batch; at eval time it uses accumulated running statistics instead, since a single inference example has no batch to normalize against. With batch size 2, the per-batch mean/variance estimates are extremely noisy, and the running statistics take longer to stabilize, producing a mismatch between train-time normalization and eval-time behavior that shows up as validation metrics not tracking training metrics reliably. Fix: increase effective batch size via gradient accumulation, or switch to GroupNorm/LayerNorm which don't depend on batch statistics at all.

drills.q: Derive the receptive field advantage of stacking two 3x3 convolutions versus one 5x5 convolution, including the parameter comparison for 64 input/output channels.
drills.a: Two stacked 3x3 convs (stride 1) reach an effective 5x5 receptive field: the first 3x3 conv's output at a given position depends on a 3x3 input window; the second 3x3 conv applied to that output depends on a 3x3 window of those outputs, which maps back to a 5x5 window of the original input. Parameters: two 3x3x64x64 convs = 2*36,864=73,728 vs one 5x5x64x64 conv = 5*5*64*64=102,400 -- fewer parameters for the same receptive field, plus an extra nonlinearity between the two smaller convs.

drills.q: A DETR-based detector needs 3x the training epochs of a Faster R-CNN baseline to reach comparable mAP, and a stakeholder wants faster iteration. What's your recommendation and why?
drills.a: Switch to a deformable-attention DETR variant (e.g. Deformable DETR), which restricts attention to a small set of learned sampling points near each query's reference location instead of full global attention. This directly addresses DETR's known slow-convergence limitation (a documented consequence of its bipartite-matching + global-attention training dynamics) while keeping the anchor-free, NMS-free framing that made DETR attractive in the first place, and it also tends to improve small-object performance as a side benefit.
